course.title: Claude Deep Dive
course.subtitle: Master Claude. Build With Claude. Work With Claude.
course.description: A hands-on, self-paced course where you learn to use Claude as a complete work system — not just a chat window. From choosing the right surface for a task to building tools, delegating work, and designing multi-step workflows, you'll build real, usable output in every module.
course.whoFor: Professionals, freelancers, students, and business owners who already use Claude occasionally and want to become genuinely capable with it — able to choose the right approach for any task, not just chat.

modules.title: Choosing Your Claude Surface
outcomes: Use the Surface Selector to decide which Claude surface actually fits a task
Understand the real difference between Chat, Connectors, Projects, Skills, Artifacts, Claude Code, Cowork, and Claude Design
Practice sorting real, messy tasks into the right surface, not just the familiar one
Walk away with a working mental model every later module builds directly on

screens.heading: Most people only ever use one-tenth of what Claude can do
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **surface selection** — the decision skill that determines whether you use Chat, Connectors, Projects, Skills, Artifacts, Claude Code, Cowork, or Claude Design for a given task.

Almost everyone who uses Claude starts and stays in the chat window — ask a question, get an answer, repeat. That's not wrong, but it's like owning a full toolbox and only ever reaching for the same screwdriver. Claude has at least eight genuinely different ways of working, and the skill that separates a casual user from someone who's actually mastered it isn't knowing more prompts — it's knowing **which surface a task actually needs**.
You'll work through this course alongside three people:

list.label: Ritika
list.text: a university student building her first real system for research and coursework instead of ad-hoc chatting.

list.label: Karan
list.text: runs operations at a small business, drowning in recurring reports and one-off requests he keeps solving from scratch.

list.label: Takshika
list.text: designs training content and keeps rebuilding the same kinds of materials without a repeatable system.

body: None of them need to learn a new AI tool. They need to learn to use the one they already have, properly.

screens.description: Before any framework, a 60-second tour of where things actually live in Claude's interface. You'll use this map in every module from here forward — verified against Claude's current Help Center, though your exact screen may vary slightly if Anthropic has updated the layout since this was written, in which case check your own Settings menu for the closest match.
steps: Look at the left sidebar — this is home base. It holds your chat history, your Projects, and a dedicated Artifacts section. If it's not visible, click the sidebar icon in the top-left corner, or press Ctrl+. (Cmd+. on Mac) to open it.
The message box in the center-bottom is where every conversation starts — that's plain Chat, the surface you already know.
Near the message box, look for a "+" icon or a "Search and tools" button — this is where you attach files, and where Connectors live. You'll use this constantly starting in Module 2.
Click your initials/profile icon in the bottom-left corner to open Settings — this is where you manage Connectors, turn on features like Artifacts under Capabilities, and adjust account details.

When Claude creates something substantial — a document, an interactive tool, code — it opens in a dedicated panel to the right of your chat, not buried inside the conversation text. That's an Artifact, covered fully in Module 6.
Keep this screen in mind as later modules say "click here" or "go to Settings" — this is the map those instructions are pointing at.

screens.heading: The Surface Selector
body: Four questions, asked in order, before you touch anything:

list.label: 1. Am I thinking, or am I making?
list.text: a conversation that ends in an answer is different from a task that needs to produce a file, a tool, or a piece of code.

list.label: 2. Is this a one-time need, or something I'll do again?
list.text: a single question doesn't deserve the same setup as something you'll repeat weekly.

list.label: 3. Does this need real, current, outside information?
list.text: Claude's own reasoning is different from Claude pulling in your actual inbox, your actual documents, or today's news.

list.label: 4. Does someone need to review this before anything happens, or can it run on its own?
list.text: a draft you'll read is different from a multi-step task you're comfortable delegating.

body: Answer these four honestly for any task, and the right surface almost picks itself. The rest of this module is just learning what each answer actually points to.

screens.heading: Where each answer actually points
body: Here's the map connecting your answers to real Claude surfaces — you'll go deep on each one across the rest of this course, this is just the overview:

list.label: Thinking, one-time, no outside data
list.text: → plain Chat. The most common need, and the one people already know.

list.label: Thinking, but needs real current information
list.text: → Connectors (your own tools) or Web Search/Research (the wider internet).

list.label: Something you'll do again and again
list.text: → a Project (persistent context) or a Skill (a repeatable process), or Memory for standing personal facts.

list.label: Making a tangible file — a report, sheet, or deck
list.text: → File Creation.

list.label: Making an interactive tool or mini-app
list.text: → Artifacts.

list.label: Making real code, scripts, or local automation
list.text: → Claude Code.

list.label: Making a visual prototype or design system
list.text: → Claude Design.

list.label: Multi-step execution you're comfortable delegating
list.text: → Cowork.

screens.heading: The same four questions, three completely different people
body: The Surface Selector isn't specific to any one profession — the same four questions produce different, equally valid answers depending on who's asking. That's the actual point of this course: **not one narrow way to use Claude, but real depth across however you actually work.**

list.label: A student
list.text: researching a term paper asks: is this recurring across the semester, or just this one paper? Does it need current academic sources? The answers usually point to Research/Web Search wrapped in a short-lived Project.

list.label: A small business owner
list.text: handling weekly supplier invoices asks the same four questions and lands somewhere completely different: recurring, needs real data from a connected accounting tool, wants review before anything is finalized — pointing to Connectors feeding a Skill.

list.label: An IT professional
list.text: triaging recurring bug reports asks the same questions again and lands on yet another answer: needs live data from a connected ticketing system, plus enough complexity that a repeatable Skill or even Claude Code makes sense for the recurring parts.

body: Same framework, three genuinely different real jobs, three different correct answers. Every module from here forward will show you this same breadth — a feature explained once, then applied across how differently people actually use it.

screens.question: True or False: If a task is something you'll need to do every single week, plain Chat is still the best surface, since you can just repeat the same question each time.

options.text: True
False

screens.explanation: False — this is exactly what Question 2 of the Surface Selector is for. A recurring need is a strong signal to set up a Project or a Skill once, so you're not manually re-explaining context every single time. Plain Chat is right for genuinely one-off needs, not repeated ones.

screens.heading: Walking Karan's task through all four questions
body: Karan needs a weekly summary of last week's sales numbers, pulled from his team's shared spreadsheet, formatted the same way every time for his manager.

list.label: Q1 — Thinking or making?
list.text: Making — it ends in a formatted summary, not just an answer in chat.

list.label: Q2 — One-time or recurring?
list.text: Recurring, every single week — a strong signal against starting from scratch each time.

list.label: Q3 — Needs real outside data?
list.text: Yes — the actual current spreadsheet numbers, not Claude's general knowledge.

list.label: Q4 — Needs review, or can it run on its own?
list.text: Karan wants to review it before it goes to his manager — at least for now.

body: Answer: this points toward a **Connector** (to read the live spreadsheet) feeding into a **Skill** (the repeatable formatting process), with Karan still reviewing before it's sent — not yet a fully autonomous Cowork task. You'll build exactly this kind of workflow in later modules.

screens.question: Which of these are genuinely true about the difference between a Project, a Skill, and Memory? Select all that apply.

options.text: A Project holds context specific to one piece of ongoing work
A Skill is a repeatable process or framework you want applied consistently
Memory is best for standing personal facts that apply across everything you do, not just one project
All three do exactly the same thing, just with different names

screens.explanation: Projects, Skills, and Memory all solve the persistence problem from Question 2, but at different scopes: a Project is tied to one specific piece of ongoing work, a Skill is a reusable process you'd apply across multiple different projects, and Memory holds standing facts about you or your preferences that should inform everything, not just one task. You'll build all three in Module 5.

screens.heading: Walking Ritika's task through the same four questions
body: Ritika has a one-off assignment: research a specific historical event for a term paper due in two weeks, pulling from multiple academic sources.

list.label: Q1 — Thinking or making?
list.text: Mostly thinking — she needs synthesized understanding, with a written report as the final output.

list.label: Q2 — One-time or recurring?
list.text: One-time, for this specific assignment.

list.label: Q3 — Needs real outside data?
list.text: Yes — multiple current, credible sources beyond what Claude already knows.

list.label: Q4 — Review or autonomous?
list.text: She'll review everything before it goes in her paper — this is coursework, not something to submit unread.

body: Answer: **Research/Web Search** for the source-gathering, likely wrapped in a temporary **Project** just for this assignment (since it'll take a few sessions, but ends when the paper's submitted) — not a permanent Skill, since this exact task won't repeat.

screens.instruction: Put the Surface Selector's four questions in the correct order.

items.text: Am I thinking, or am I making?
Is this a one-time need, or something I'll do again?
Does this need real, current, outside information?
Does someone need to review this, or can it run on its own?

screens.explanation: This order matters because each question narrows the field before the next one applies — deciding thinking-vs-making first rules out entire surfaces before you even consider recurrence, data needs, or autonomy.

screens.heading: Build your own surface-selection prompt
body: When you're genuinely unsure which surface fits, you can ask Claude itself to help triage — but only if you give it the right structure. Fill in the blanks below to build that prompt yourself, the same way you'll do with real prompts throughout this course.

screens.heading: Complete the surface-triage prompt
screens.template: I have a task that is [[1]] rather than a one-off, [[2]] real current information, and [[3]] before anything happens. Given this, which Claude surface would you recommend and why?
screens.explanation: This assembled prompt hands Claude exactly the three signals from the Surface Selector — recurrence, data needs, and review requirements — instead of a vague "what should I use for this?" A vague question gets a vague answer; a structured one gets a structured recommendation you can actually act on.

screens.heading: Your turn — triage one of your own real tasks
screens.prompt: I have a task that is [recurring / one-time] rather than [the opposite], [requires / doesn't require] real current information from outside sources, and [needs my review / can run on its own] before anything happens. Here's the task itself: [describe your actual task in 2-3 sentences]. Given this, which Claude surface would you recommend and why?
screens.examplePrompt: I have a task that is recurring rather than one-time, requires real current information from outside sources, and needs my review before anything happens. Here's the task: every Friday I need to check my team's shared project tracker and write a short summary of what's overdue for my manager. Given this, which Claude surface would you recommend and why?
screens.note: Pick a real task you actually do, not a hypothetical one — the whole point of this exercise is testing the framework against something true, so you can trust it on the next 11 modules' worth of real tasks.

screens.heading: The two mistakes almost everyone makes

list.label: Defaulting to Chat for everything
list.text: the most common mistake — treating every task, including genuinely recurring ones, as a fresh conversation. This means re-explaining context every single time, and losing consistency across attempts.

list.label: Over-formalizing simple, one-off tasks
list.text: the opposite mistake, less common but real — building a whole Project or Skill for something you'll only ever do once. This wastes setup time for zero future benefit.

body: ==The Surface Selector exists precisely to catch both mistakes== — it forces you to actually check recurrence and complexity instead of defaulting to whichever surface is most familiar or most impressive-sounding.

screens.question: Takshika builds a brand-new Project every single time she needs to write one training email, even though she never reuses it afterward. Which mistake is this?

options.text: Defaulting to Chat for everything
Over-formalizing a simple, one-off task
This isn't a mistake — more structure is always better
Using Claude Code instead of Chat

screens.explanation: Setting up a Project makes sense when the context will be reused across multiple sessions. A single, one-off email doesn't need that overhead — plain Chat, or at most a quick reusable prompt, would get the same result with far less setup time.

items: The **Surface Selector** — thinking vs. making, one-time vs. recurring, needs outside data or not, needs review or not — decides which Claude surface actually fits a task.
**Chat is the default everyone knows**, but it's only the right answer for genuinely one-off, self-contained thinking tasks.
**Recurring work deserves a Project or Skill**; genuinely one-off work doesn't need that setup overhead.
This framework isn't the end of the course — it's the **lens** every later module's capability gets viewed through.

screens.heading: What you built, and what's next
body: You now have a working framework for deciding which Claude surface fits any task — and you've already tested it against a real task of your own.

**Module 2** goes deep on the first surface most people underuse: **Connectors** — how to actually bring your real work (email, documents, project trackers) into a Claude conversation, and how to catch it when a Connector pulls in the wrong information.

modules.title: Bringing Real Work In
outcomes: Understand deeply what Connectors are, why they exist, and exactly how they work under the hood
Build a real practice file, connect it to Claude, and query it — one complete live example, start to finish
See real, practical Connector use cases across students, business owners, IT professionals, and freelancers
Use the Connector Audit to catch bad pulls, and know when manual upload beats a Connector entirely

screens.heading: Question 3 of the Surface Selector, answered in full
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **Connectors**.

In Module 1, Question 3 asked whether a task needs real, current, outside information. When the answer is yes, and that information lives inside tools you already use, a Connector is how Claude reaches it, instead of you copy-pasting it in by hand every time.
This module isn't just concepts — you're going to build one real, live example from scratch: create an actual file, connect it, and query it, exactly the way you would for real work.

screens.heading: What a Connector actually does
body: A Connector gives Claude permission to read from a specific external source you've linked — email, documents, calendars, project trackers, and similar work tools, depending on what's available in your workspace and plan.

**Exact available connectors vary by plan and workspace setup** — check your own Claude settings for what's currently connected before assuming a specific tool is available; this list changes as Anthropic adds support for more services.

What a Connector does **not** do: it doesn't act on your behalf inside that tool. This distinction matters a lot more once we get to Cowork in Module 8 — for now, treat Connectors as read access, not control.

screens.description: Step 1 of your live example: create the actual file you'll connect. We're using Google Sheets — a simple project tracker — since it's free, familiar, and lets you see real query results against real data you built yourself.
steps: Go to sheets.google.com and click the blank spreadsheet ("+") to create a new one.
Rename it "My Project Tracker" (click the title at the top-left and type the new name).
In row 1, create four column headers: type "Serial No" in cell A1, "Task Name" in B1, "Status" in C1, and "Risk" in D1.
Now fill in 5 rows of practice data below the headers, exactly as shown:
Row 2: 1 | Update client proposal | In Progress | Medium
Row 3: 2 | Vendor contract renewal | Not Started | High
Row 4: 3 | Team onboarding docs | Completed | Low
Row 5: 4 | Q3 budget review | In Progress | High
Row 6: 5 | Website content refresh | Not Started | Low
This file is now sitting in your Google Drive automatically — Sheets saves as you type, no separate save step needed.

screens.description: Step 2: connect Google Drive to Claude — this is the general connector setup, click by click, verified against Claude's current Help Center.
steps: In Claude, click your profile icon (your initials, bottom-left corner) → Settings → Connectors. Or, inside any chat, click the "+" icon near the message box.
Find "Google Drive" in the connector directory (search or scroll — it's usually under a Google Workspace or Productivity category).
Click "Connect" next to it.

You'll be redirected to Google's own login screen. Sign in with the same Google account you used to create your tracker, and review the permissions Claude is requesting — this is the Scope check from the Connector Audit, happening live.
Approve the permissions. You're returned to Claude, and Google Drive is now connected.

screens.description: Step 3: this is the part most guides skip — actually selecting your specific file so Claude knows exactly which one you mean, not just "somewhere in Drive." Two ways to do this, verified against Claude's official documentation:
steps: Method 1 — inside a Project (the officially documented path): create or open a Project, find the "Files" or "Project Knowledge" section, click "Add Content" → "Google Drive," then either search your recent documents for "My Project Tracker" or paste its Google Sheets URL directly. Click it to add it to that Project's knowledge.

Method 2 — inside a normal chat: once Google Drive is connected, you can often reference a file directly by typing @ followed by the file name (e.g. @My Project Tracker) right in your message, and selecting it from the list that appears.

If neither option looks exactly like this on your screen, your interface may have updated since this was written — look for "Add Content," "Files," or an @ symbol near the message box, since one of these is almost certainly how your version handles it.

One honest limitation worth knowing now: Claude can read and analyze your tracker through this connection, but it cannot directly edit, update, or add rows to the existing file — that's a different capability, covered when we reach Skills and Cowork later in this course.

screens.promptLabel: Step 4: query your actual tracker
screens.prompt: Using my connected Google Drive, find the file named "My Project Tracker" and tell me: which tasks are marked as High risk this week, and what their current status is.
screens.examplePrompt: Using my connected Google Drive, find the file named "My Project Tracker" and tell me: which tasks are marked as High risk this week, and what their current status is.
screens.output: Found your file "My Project Tracker." Two tasks are marked High risk: "Vendor contract renewal" (Status: Not Started) and "Q3 budget review" (Status: In Progress). Both are worth flagging as priorities this week, since High risk combined with incomplete status is exactly the combination that tends to become a real problem if left unaddressed.
screens.explanation: If you built the tracker exactly as shown, you should see this same result — genuine proof the connection is working end to end, not something you have to take on faith. This is the whole loop: create real data, connect it, ask a real question, get a real, verifiable answer.

screens.question: You just asked Claude to update the Status of "Vendor contract renewal" to "Completed" directly in your tracker. What happens?

options.text: Claude updates the cell in your Google Sheet immediately
Claude can't make this edit through the Drive connector — it can only read the file, not write to it
Claude deletes the row instead
Nothing happens, no response at all

screens.explanation: This is the read-only limitation from Step 3 — the Google Drive connector lets Claude read and analyze your tracker, but not edit the existing file. Claude will likely explain this and may offer to show you what the updated data would look like, or generate a new file, rather than silently failing or pretending to have made the change.

screens.heading: Real breadth: who else uses Connectors, and for what
body: You just connected one file for one purpose. The same underlying pattern — create or use a real source, connect it, ask a real question — applies across very different working lives:

list.label: A student
list.text: connects a documents/research folder to pull together sources for a paper; connects email to track application deadlines across a busy inbox without missing one.

list.label: A small business owner
list.text: connects an accounting or invoicing tool for a plain-language weekly cash-flow summary; connects a shared calendar to check for double-bookings before confirming a client meeting.

list.label: An IT professional
list.text: connects a ticketing system to triage what's actually urgent versus just noisy; connects a code repository's issue tracker to draft a weekly status update automatically.

list.label: A freelancer or marketer
list.text: connects a project management tool to check which deliverables are approaching deadline; connects analytics to get a plain-English summary instead of a dashboard full of numbers.

body: None of these are exotic. They're the boring, recurring, slightly tedious parts of real work — exactly where a Connector earns its keep, the same way your tracker just did.

screens.heading: The Connector Audit
body: Before you trust anything a Connector pulled in, check three things — you actually just did the first one, in Step 2:

list.label: Scope
list.text: did Claude actually have permission to see the specific thing you needed? You reviewed exactly this during the Google sign-in step.

list.label: Source
list.text: which exact document, channel, or record did this come from? "My Project Tracker" only worked because you named it specifically.

list.label: Staleness
list.text: how current is this, really? A Connector pulling from a document last edited two months ago will confidently hand you two-month-old information as if it were today's.

body: ==Most Connector failures aren't the Connector malfunctioning — they're one of these three going unchecked.==

screens.heading: Prompt Lab: Combining more than one source
body: Your tracker example used one source. The real power shows up combining more than one — something no single source has on its own.

body.prompt: Using [connected source A] and [connected source B], build a combined summary of [what you need]. Cross-reference the two — flag anything that appears in one source but not the other, and anything that seems to contradict between them.

screens.promptLabel: Takshika combines two sources for a training content brief
screens.prompt: Using [connected source A] and [connected source B], build a combined summary of [what you need]. Cross-reference the two.
screens.examplePrompt: Using my connected email and my connected shared documents folder, build a combined summary of what stakeholders have requested for the new onboarding training. Cross-reference the two — flag anything that appears in one source but not the other, and anything that seems to contradict between them.
screens.output: Combined summary shows 5 requested topics consistent across both email threads and the shared doc. One request — a session on data privacy — appears only in a recent email, not yet reflected in the shared doc. One mild contradiction: an email specifies a 2-hour session length, while the shared doc's outline implies closer to 3 hours worth of content.
screens.explanation: This is the kind of cross-checking that would take real manual effort to do by hand. The value isn't that Claude read two sources — it's that it was explicitly asked to reconcile them, catching a real scope mismatch before it became a problem.

screens.question: Your tracker query came back saying "Vendor contract renewal" is High risk — but you actually updated it to Low risk in the sheet 10 minutes ago, and Claude's answer doesn't reflect that. Which parts of the Connector Audit does this point to?

options.text: Staleness — the pulled data may not reflect your most recent edit yet
Source — Claude may have grabbed a different file with a similar name
Scope — Claude never had permission to see the file at all
This can't happen once a Connector is set up

screens.explanation: Both are genuinely possible causes worth checking: Staleness (the read may have happened just before your edit synced), or Source (if you have more than one similarly-named tracker). Scope isn't the issue here — Claude clearly could see a file, it answered from something.

screens.heading: Reach vs. Precision: Connector or manual upload?
body: Connectors and manually uploading a file both get information into Claude — they're not interchangeable.

list.label: Connectors give you Reach
list.text: pulling from many sources, live, without re-uploading every time something changes. Best for breadth or currency — exactly what you just did with your tracker.

list.label: Manual upload gives you Precision
list.text: you know exactly which file version Claude is looking at, because you chose it yourself. Best when one specific document matters and you can't risk a similar-but-wrong file.

body: When something is genuinely high-stakes and there's any chance of a Source mix-up, manual upload of the exact file you mean is often safer than trusting a Connector to find the right one.

screens.question: Ritika needs to reference one specific final exam-prep document she wrote last week, and it's critical she's working from the exact right version. Connector or manual upload?

options.text: Connector — it's faster
Manual upload — precision matters more here than reach
Neither would work for this
It doesn't matter which one she uses

screens.explanation: This is a Precision situation: one specific, known document, where getting the exact right version matters. Manual upload removes any risk of a Connector grabbing a similarly-named but wrong file.

screens.heading: Build your own Connector Audit prompt
screens.template: Before I trust this, confirm three things: what [[1]] you actually had for this source, exactly which [[2]] this information came from, and how [[3]] it is.
screens.explanation: This turns the Connector Audit into a direct question you can ask Claude after any pull, forcing it to state its own Scope, Source, and Staleness explicitly rather than you having to infer them.

screens.heading: Your turn — extend your tracker query
screens.prompt: Using my connected Google Drive, find [file name]. Then tell me: [a different question about the same data — e.g. which tasks are still Not Started]. Also confirm: what scope/permission you had for this source, and how current the data looks.
screens.examplePrompt: Using my connected Google Drive, find "My Project Tracker." Then tell me: which tasks are still Not Started, and which of those also carry High or Medium risk. Also confirm what scope/permission you had for this source, and how current the data looks.
screens.note: Use the exact same tracker you already built — the point here is asking a second, different question against data you already trust, not building something new.

items: You built a **real, complete example** — created a file, connected it, selected it specifically, and queried it — the full loop, not just theory.
**Connectors give Claude read access**, not write access — your tracker stayed exactly as you built it.
The **Connector Audit** — Scope, Source, Staleness — catches most real failures, and you checked Scope yourself during setup.
**Connectors give Reach, manual upload gives Precision** — pick based on which one the task actually needs.

screens.heading: What you built, and what's next
body: You now have a real, working Connector example you built yourself — not just a concept, something you can point to and say "I did that."
**Module 3** covers the other half of Question 3 — when you need current information that *isn't* sitting in a file you own, but out in the wider world. That's Research, Thinking, and Web Search.

modules.title: Thinking, Researching, Verifying
outcomes: Tell Web Search, Extended Thinking, and Research apart — three genuinely different tools, not one blurry feature
Run a real, live Research task from scratch and get back a citation-backed report
Use Extended Thinking on a genuinely hard, multi-constraint problem and see the difference it makes
See real breadth of use across students, business owners, IT professionals, and freelancers

screens.heading: Three buttons most people walk past every day
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **Web Search, Extended Thinking, and Research**.

These three get confused constantly, because they all sound like "Claude gets smarter." They don't do the same thing at all. One gets you a current fact in seconds. One makes Claude reason harder through a genuinely hard problem. One runs an autonomous, multi-source investigation that can take up to 45 minutes and hands you back a real report.
Picking the wrong one wastes either your time or your patience — this module makes sure you never have to guess again.

screens.heading: Fact, Think, or Investigate?
body: One question decides which of the three you need:

list.label: Need one current fact, fast?
list.text: Web Search. A single live lookup, grounded with citations, seconds to answer.

list.label: Need Claude to reason harder through something genuinely hard?
list.text: Extended Thinking. No internet involved — just more deliberate step-by-step reasoning on a complex problem using what Claude already knows.

list.label: Need a full, multi-source investigation you can wait a few minutes for?
list.text: Research. Claude runs multiple searches, reads results, decides what to dig into next, and delivers a structured, citation-backed report — not a quick answer.

body: ==Thinking is for deliberation. Search is for facts. Research is for reports.==

screens.description: All three toggles live in roughly the same place, verified against Claude's current interface — though exact wording may vary slightly by your account and plan.
steps: For Web Search: click the "Search and tools" (slider/tools) icon near the message box, find "Web search" in the dropdown, and switch the toggle on.

For Extended Thinking: click the model name next to the send button (this opens a menu covering Model, Effort, and Thinking together) and switch the "Thinking" toggle on. On some interface versions, this same toggle instead appears inside the "Search and tools" panel — if you don't see it by the send button, check there.
For Research: click the same "Search and tools" icon and look for a "Research" option — click it to enable, click again to disable. Research requires a paid plan (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise).
You can combine these — Research automatically uses Extended Thinking internally, for example — but for this module, try them one at a time first so you can see exactly what each one does on its own.

screens.promptLabel: Web Search: a quick current fact
screens.prompt: [Ask about something genuinely current — a recent event, a live price, today's status of something]
screens.examplePrompt: What's the current weather forecast for Pune this week?
screens.output: A live, sourced forecast for the week, pulled from a current weather service — with a citation you can click to verify it yourself, rather than an answer from Claude's training data (which would have no way of knowing this week's actual forecast).
screens.explanation: This is Web Search doing exactly its one job: a single live fact, grounded and citable, in seconds. Notice this wasn't a research report — it's a fast, single-purpose lookup.

screens.question: True or False: Web Search and Research are basically the same feature, just with different names.

options.text: True
False

screens.explanation: False. Web Search does one live lookup in seconds. Research runs an autonomous multi-step investigation — multiple searches, reading and cross-referencing results, deciding what to dig into next — that can take several minutes and produces a structured report, not a quick answer.

screens.heading: Prompt Lab: A genuinely hard problem for Extended Thinking
body: Extended Thinking earns its keep on problems with real, competing constraints — not simple questions. A good test: something with three or more conditions that all have to be satisfied together.

body.prompt: I need to schedule [X people/tasks] across [Y time slots], with these constraints: [list 3 or more real constraints, some of which conflict]. Work through this step by step and give me a schedule that satisfies as many constraints as possible, and clearly flag any constraint you had to compromise on and why.

screens.promptLabel: Karan uses Extended Thinking for a real scheduling conflict
screens.prompt: I need to schedule [X] across [Y], with these constraints: [list 3+ constraints]. Work through this step by step and flag any compromise.
screens.examplePrompt: I need to schedule 4 team members across 3 shifts this week, with these constraints: no one works two shifts in a row, at least one senior person must be on every shift, one team member is unavailable on Wednesday, and total hours must stay roughly even across all 4 people. Work through this step by step and give me a schedule, flagging any constraint you had to compromise on.
screens.output: A full weekly schedule satisfying all four constraints, with an expandable Thinking section above it showing the actual reasoning: which combinations were tried and rejected, why the Wednesday gap forced a specific senior-coverage tradeoff on Thursday, and confirmation that total hours came out within one hour of perfectly even across all four people. One flagged compromise: one team member ends up with a slightly heavier Friday load, clearly explained rather than silently absorbed.
screens.explanation: This is what Extended Thinking is actually for — not a faster answer, but a demonstrably more reasoned one, with the reasoning itself visible for you to check rather than trust blindly.

screens.heading: Prompt Lab: Your flagship Research task
body: This is the main event of this module — a real, live Research task, start to finish. Pick something you'd genuinely want a thorough, sourced answer to, since this will take several minutes to run.

body.prompt: Act as a research analyst. I need a report on: [your topic]. Specifically cover: [2-4 sub-questions you actually want answered]. Compare at least [2-3] real options where relevant, cite your sources, and clearly flag anywhere the information is uncertain or could change quickly.

screens.description: Run your flagship Research task now, step by step:
steps: Click the "Search and tools" icon, find "Research," and toggle it on.
Type your Research prompt from the previous screen and send it.

You'll see a "Researching..." indicator — Claude is now running multiple searches and reading results, not writing a response yet. This can take anywhere from 5 to 45 minutes depending on how complex your question is.
You don't need to keep the tab open — Research runs in the background. Switch to something else and come back.
When it's done, you'll see a structured, citation-backed report — expand any section to see the sources behind a specific claim.

screens.promptLabel: Takshika researches training platforms for a real decision
screens.prompt: Act as a research analyst. I need a report on: [topic]. Cover: [sub-questions]. Compare [2-3] real options, cite sources, flag uncertainty.
screens.examplePrompt: Act as a research analyst. I need a report on free and low-cost platforms for hosting employee training content. Cover: what each platform actually supports (video, quizzes, tracking completion), pricing at a small-team scale, and any known limitations. Compare at least 3 real options, cite your sources, and flag anywhere the information could change quickly (like pricing).
screens.outputLabel: What Claude gives back, after a few minutes
screens.output: A structured report comparing 3 real platforms across the requested dimensions — features, small-team pricing, and limitations — each claim backed by a clickable citation. A clear note flags that pricing specifically should be re-verified directly before making a final decision, since it's the kind of detail that shifts without much notice. The report ends with a short summary recommendation based on the stated priorities, not just a raw comparison table.
screens.explanation: Compare this to the single-fact Web Search example from earlier — this is a genuinely different kind of output: a synthesized, sourced, decision-ready report, not a quick lookup. That difference is the entire reason Research exists as its own separate tool.

screens.question: Which of these are real differences between Research and a quick Web Search? Select all that apply.

options.text: Research runs multiple searches and decides what to investigate next; Web Search does one lookup
Research can take several minutes to complete; Web Search answers in seconds
Research produces a structured, multi-source report; Web Search gives a direct answer to one question
There is no real difference between them

screens.explanation: All three are genuine, verified differences. Research is fundamentally a different kind of tool — autonomous, multi-step, slower, and built for depth — not just a slower version of Web Search.

screens.heading: Verifying what comes back
body: Citations don't mean unquestionable. Before treating any Web Search or Research output as settled:

list.label: Check the source type
list.text: a citation from an official source (a company's own pricing page, a government site) is stronger than a citation from a random blog repeating secondhand information.

list.label: Check for a flagged uncertainty
list.text: if Claude explicitly says something could be outdated or disputed, take that seriously rather than skimming past it.

list.label: Re-verify anything time-sensitive before acting
list.text: pricing, availability, and "current" anything is exactly the category most likely to have shifted between when Research ran and when you actually act on it.

screens.question: A Research report cites a company's official pricing page from a search 20 minutes ago, and flags: "verify current pricing before finalizing, as this can change without notice." What should you do?

options.text: Ignore the note — 20 minutes ago is basically current
Treat this seriously and do a quick re-check before making a final decision, especially since Claude itself flagged the uncertainty
Distrust the entire report because of one flagged note
Assume the flag is just a generic disclaimer with no real meaning

screens.explanation: A flagged uncertainty in a Research report is a genuine signal, not boilerplate — it means Claude itself identified this specific detail as likely to shift. Take it at face value: quick re-check before anything final, not blind trust and not blanket distrust of the whole report.

list.label: A student
list.text: uses Web Search for a quick current fact for an assignment; uses Research to compare universities or scholarship programs across multiple criteria before applying.

list.label: A small business owner
list.text: uses Web Search to check a competitor's current pricing; uses Research to fully evaluate 3 accounting software options before switching.

list.label: An IT professional
list.text: uses Extended Thinking to work through a genuinely tricky multi-constraint system design problem; uses Research to compare current best practices across several real-world implementations.

list.label: A freelancer
list.text: uses Web Search to check current freelance rate benchmarks; uses Research to build a full comparison of project management tools before committing to one.

screens.instruction: Put these in order from fastest to slowest.

items.text: Web Search — a single live lookup
Extended Thinking — deeper reasoning, no internet
Research — multi-step investigation with a full report

screens.explanation: Web Search is the fastest — one lookup, seconds. Extended Thinking takes a bit longer since it's reasoning more deliberately, but it's not searching the web. Research is by far the slowest — genuinely minutes, sometimes up to 45 — because it's running an entire multi-step investigation.

screens.heading: Build your own tool-selection check
screens.template: I need [[1]] because this requires [[2]], and I'm prepared to wait [[3]] for the result.
screens.explanation: This is the Fact/Think/Investigate check turned into a sentence you can literally say to yourself before picking a toggle — matching the tool to both the task and the time you're actually willing to spend.

screens.heading: Your turn — run one more Research task
screens.prompt: Act as a research analyst. I need a report on: [your real topic]. Cover: [2-4 sub-questions]. Compare [2-3] real options, cite sources, flag uncertainty.
screens.examplePrompt: Act as a research analyst. I need a report on the best free note-taking apps for university students. Cover: core features, sync across devices, and any real limitations of the free tier. Compare at least 3 real options, cite your sources.
screens.note: Pick a real question you actually want answered — the point of this exercise is a genuinely useful report you'll actually use, not a throwaway test.

items: **Web Search** is for one current fact, fast. **Extended Thinking** is for reasoning harder through a hard problem, no internet needed. **Research** is for a full, multi-source, citation-backed report.
The rule of thumb: **thinking is for deliberation, search is for facts, research is for reports.**
A flagged uncertainty in a Research report is a genuine signal worth re-checking, especially for anything time-sensitive like pricing.
Research can take several minutes — it runs in the background, so start it and come back rather than waiting on the tab.

screens.heading: From chat text to a file you can actually send
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **File Creation** — real Word documents, Excel spreadsheets, and PowerPoint presentations, downloadable and ready to use.

This is genuinely available to everyone — free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise — with no special setup or toggle required, verified against Claude's current Help Center. You just describe what you want in plain language, and Claude builds the actual file, running code behind the scenes in a private environment to produce it.

One thing worth knowing upfront so you don't confuse the two: this in-chat file creation is different from the separate Claude Office add-ins that live inside Word, Excel, and PowerPoint themselves — those require a paid plan and a separate install. This module covers the simpler, always-available in-chat version, which is what most people actually need.

screens.heading: Shape, Fill, Finish
body: The single biggest reason a generated file comes back wrong isn't a Claude limitation — it's an underspecified prompt. Three things to always include:

list.label: Shape
list.text: the structure — how many sections, sheets, or slides, and what each one is for. "A budget tracker" is vague; "a budget tracker with a Monthly Entries sheet and a separate Summary Dashboard sheet" is a shape.

list.label: Fill
list.text: the actual content or data — real numbers, real categories, real text, not placeholders you'll have to replace yourself afterward.

list.label: Finish
list.text: formatting and style expectations — tone for a document, whether a spreadsheet needs working formulas or just numbers, how many words per slide.

body: ==Describe the structure, not just the topic — that's the entire difference between a usable first draft and a five-round back-and-forth.==

screens.description: How to actually get a file, start to finish — the same basic flow for Word, Excel, or PowerPoint.
steps: In any chat, describe the file you want using Shape, Fill, and Finish — no special toggle or settings needed first.
Claude works in a private, sandboxed environment to actually build the file — you'll see an indicator that it's working, similar to how a code task runs.
When it's done, a download card appears directly in the conversation.
Click it to download the file to your device, or use the option to save it directly to Google Drive if that's available in your interface.
Open it in the real application (Word, Excel, PowerPoint) to check it — always verify formatting and formulas rather than assuming the download is final.

screens.heading: Flagship example 1: a real Word document

body.prompt: Create a Word document: a one-page project status update. Shape: title, a 2-3 sentence summary, a bulleted "What's done" section, a bulleted "What's next" section, and a short "Risks" section. Fill: [paste your real project details — what's actually done, what's next, any real risk]. Finish: professional but not overly formal tone, use bold for section headers.

screens.promptLabel: Karan generates a real status update
screens.prompt: Create a Word document: a one-page project status update. Shape: [structure]. Fill: [real details]. Finish: [style].
screens.examplePrompt: Create a Word document: a one-page project status update. Shape: title, a 2-3 sentence summary, a bulleted "What's done" section, a bulleted "What's next" section, and a short "Risks" section. Fill: vendor contract renewal completed this week; delivery-risk tracker now covers all 6 vendors; next is rolling out the tracker to a second team; risk is one vendor's data feed has been inconsistent for 3 days. Finish: professional but not overly formal, bold section headers.
screens.output: A downloadable .docx file with a clean title, a short summary paragraph, and three clearly bolded sections — What's Done, What's Next, and Risks — each with the real bullet points supplied, formatted as an actual Word document with proper heading styles, not just plain text with asterisks.
screens.explanation: Notice the output isn't placeholder text needing edits — because Shape, Fill, and Finish were all specified, Karan gets something close to send-ready on the first try, not a template to rebuild.

options.text: True
False

screens.heading: Flagship example 2: a real Excel spreadsheet with working formulas

body.prompt: Create an Excel spreadsheet: [what you're tracking]. Shape: [X] columns — [name them] — plus a separate summary sheet with totals. Fill: [real sample data, at least 5-8 rows]. Finish: use an actual SUM formula for totals, not just typed numbers, and apply basic conditional formatting to flag [a specific condition].

screens.promptLabel: Takshika builds a real training budget tracker
screens.prompt: Create an Excel spreadsheet: [what you're tracking]. Shape: [columns] plus a summary sheet. Fill: [real data]. Finish: [formulas/formatting requirements].
screens.examplePrompt: Create an Excel spreadsheet: a training budget tracker. Shape: columns for Item, Category, Budgeted Cost, Actual Cost, Variance, plus a separate summary sheet with totals by category. Fill: 6 real line items across venue, materials, and facilitator fees, with realistic numbers. Finish: use an actual formula for Variance (Actual minus Budgeted) and for the category totals, and apply conditional formatting to highlight any row where Actual exceeds Budgeted in red.
screens.output: A downloadable .xlsx file with two sheets — a detail sheet with all 6 line items and a working Variance formula in each row (not typed numbers), and a Summary sheet with SUM formulas totaling each category automatically. Two rows where actual cost exceeded budget are highlighted in red via real conditional formatting, visible immediately on opening the file in Excel.
screens.explanation: The formulas are the real test here — open this file and change one number, and the Variance and totals recalculate automatically, exactly like a spreadsheet you built by hand. That's a genuinely different, more useful output than a static table of numbers.

screens.question: Which of these are genuine current capabilities of Claude's file creation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Creating an Excel file with real, working formulas
Applying conditional formatting based on a rule you specify
Generating a PowerPoint deck from a document or notes
Requires a paid plan for any file type, even the basic in-chat version

screens.explanation: The first three are all genuine, verified capabilities. The fourth is false — basic in-chat file creation (Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF) is available to all users including the free plan; only the separate Office add-ins require a paid plan.

screens.heading: Flagship example 3: a real PowerPoint deck

body.prompt: Create a PowerPoint presentation: [topic], for [audience]. Shape: [X] slides — one main idea per slide. Fill: [real content — paste notes, a document, or list your key points]. Finish: [tone/style — e.g. clean and minimal, one idea per slide, no dense paragraphs].

screens.promptLabel: Ritika turns study notes into a presentation
screens.prompt: Create a PowerPoint presentation: [topic], for [audience]. Shape: [X] slides. Fill: [real content]. Finish: [style].
screens.examplePrompt: Create a PowerPoint presentation: an overview of my research paper's main argument, for my class presentation. Shape: 6 slides — title, thesis, 3 supporting points, and a conclusion — one main idea per slide. Fill: [pasted her actual paper's thesis and 3 key arguments]. Finish: clean and minimal, no dense paragraphs, short phrases only.
screens.output: A downloadable .pptx file with 6 slides matching exactly the requested structure — a title slide, one slide per supporting point with short phrases rather than full paragraphs, and a conclusion slide. Genuinely editable in PowerPoint afterward, not an image or a locked format.
screens.explanation: Because the Shape (6 slides, one idea each) and Finish (short phrases, minimal) were both specified up front, Ritika didn't get the common AI-slide problem of dense, paragraph-heavy slides that need a full rewrite before she can present them.

screens.heading: Before you send any generated file onward

list.label: Open it in the real application
list.text: don't trust a preview alone — a Word doc's heading styles, an Excel formula, or a PowerPoint's layout can look right in a quick glance and still need a check in the actual software.

list.label: Check formulas by changing one number
list.text: if a spreadsheet's totals don't update when you edit a value, something didn't generate as a real formula.

list.label: Read every slide, not just the first one
list.text: AI-generated decks sometimes front-load quality on the first few slides — check the whole thing before presenting it.

screens.question: You generate an Excel budget tracker, open it, and the numbers look right at a glance. What's the fastest real check that the formulas are genuinely working, not just typed-in numbers?

options.text: Trust it — if the numbers look right, they're right
Change one input value and see whether the totals automatically update
Re-download the file and compare it to itself
Ask Claude if the formulas are real

screens.explanation: This is the one genuinely fast, reliable test — a real formula recalculates the moment you change an input; a typed static number never will, no matter how correct it looked before you touched it.

**Module 5** shifts from one-off outputs to something that persists: Projects, Memory, and Skills, and how they work together to make Claude feel personalized to your actual work instead of starting fresh every conversation.

modules.title: Personalizing Claude
outcomes: Understand the Personalization Stack — Memory, Project, and Skill — and when each one actually fits
Set up one real Project, add one real Memory fact, and build one real Skill — a complete flagship example
Stop re-explaining yourself every conversation, using the right layer for the right kind of context
See real breadth of use across students, business owners, IT professionals, and freelancers

screens.heading: The blank-slate problem
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **Projects, Memory, and Skills**.

Every new Claude conversation starts cold by default — no memory of your tone preferences, no context on your ongoing work, no awareness of the process you use every week. That's fine for a single quick question. It's genuinely wasteful for anything you do more than once.

This module fixes that with one live, connected example: you'll set up a real Project, teach Claude one real fact about yourself through Memory, and build one real reusable Skill — three different tools for three different kinds of "don't make me repeat myself."

screens.heading: The Personalization Stack
body: Three layers, each solving a different scope of repetition:

list.label: Memory — about you
list.text: standing facts that should apply everywhere: your job, your writing style, your general preferences. Set once, used in every conversation, regardless of topic.

list.label: Project — about this work
list.text: context specific to one ongoing piece of work: a client, a course, a specific initiative. Scoped — it doesn't leak into unrelated conversations.

list.label: Skill — about this process
list.text: a repeatable way of doing a specific task, reusable across different projects and contexts. Not about you or one project — about a procedure.

body: ==Get the scope wrong and you'll either re-explain yourself constantly, or pollute every conversation with context that only belonged to one piece of work.==

screens.description: Flagship example, part 1: create a real Project. Verified against Claude's current Help Center — Projects are available to all users now, free plan included (up to 5 Projects on free; unlimited on paid plans).
steps: Hover over the left side of your account and click "Projects," or go directly to claude.ai/projects.
Click "+ New Project" in the upper right corner.
Give it a specific, real name — not "Work Stuff." For this exercise, name it something like "Client Onboarding" or whatever real ongoing work you actually have.
You'll find the project knowledge base on the right side of the project's main page. Click the "+" button there to upload any real documents relevant to this work — a template, a brief, past notes.
Click "Set project instructions" and write a short instruction for how Claude should behave specifically within this Project — for example, a particular tone or a standing rule for this work.
Save. From now on, starting a new chat inside this Project carries all of this context automatically — no re-explaining.

screens.promptLabel: Karan sets up a real Project for client onboarding
screens.prompt: [Project instructions field] Act as my onboarding assistant for new clients. Keep all communication warm but efficient — no long paragraphs. Every new client needs: a welcome email, a kickoff call agenda, and a project timeline template.
screens.examplePrompt: [Project instructions field] Act as my onboarding assistant for new clients. Keep all communication warm but efficient — no long paragraphs. Every new client needs: a welcome email, a kickoff call agenda, and a project timeline template.
screens.output: From this point forward, any new chat started inside the "Client Onboarding" Project already knows Karan's tone preference and the standard three deliverables, without him typing any of it again. Asking simply "draft the welcome email for a new client named Priya" inside this Project produces something already matching the house style — because the Project instructions supplied the context automatically.
screens.explanation: This is the entire point of a Project: context set once, reused every single time you work inside it, without re-explaining anything.

screens.question: True or False: Projects require a paid Claude plan — there's no way to use them on the free tier.

options.text: True
False

screens.explanation: False — Projects are available on the free plan, capped at 5 Projects. Paid plans (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise) get unlimited Projects plus additional features like expanded knowledge capacity and organization sharing.

screens.description: Flagship example, part 2: teach Claude one real fact through Memory. One honest note before you start — Claude currently has two possible interface versions depending on your account, so check both if the first one isn't where you expect it.
steps: Click your profile icon (bottom-left corner) → Settings.
Look for a section called "Memory" directly in the Settings menu — if you see it, turn on "Generate memory from chats" there. This is the newer interface.

If you don't see "Memory" directly, instead go to Settings → Capabilities, and scroll to the Memory section there — this is the older (legacy) interface, and works the same way, just laid out differently.
Once enabled, memory builds automatically from your conversations going forward — it does not look backward at chats from before you turned it on.

To add something manually right now instead of waiting for it to build naturally, look for a pencil/edit icon in the memory view, and write a direct fact — e.g. "I run a small business and prefer concise, no-fluff written communication."

screens.promptLabel: Karan adds one real Memory fact
screens.prompt: [Manually added memory entry] I run a small operations-focused business. I prefer concise, no-fluff written communication — get to the point in the first sentence.
screens.examplePrompt: [Manually added memory entry] I run a small operations-focused business. I prefer concise, no-fluff written communication — get to the point in the first sentence.
screens.output: Unlike the Project instructions (which only apply inside "Client Onboarding"), this fact now applies in every conversation Karan has with Claude, on any topic — a completely unrelated chat about a personal errand will still get the same concise, no-fluff tone, because Memory is about him, not about one piece of work.
screens.explanation: This is the real test of whether something belongs in Memory versus a Project: would this be true and useful in a completely unrelated conversation? If yes, Memory. If it only makes sense for one specific piece of work, it belongs in that Project instead.

screens.question: Which of these genuinely belong in Memory rather than a specific Project? Select all that apply.

options.text: "I prefer bullet points over long paragraphs in every response"
"This specific client, Priya, wants weekly check-ins on Fridays"
"I work in marketing and always want examples relevant to that field"
"The Q3 budget for this specific project is capped at 50,000"

screens.explanation: A and C are true about you regardless of context — general formatting preference and professional field — so they belong in Memory. B and D are specific to one piece of work (one client, one project's budget) and belong inside that Project's instructions instead, not in general Memory.

screens.description: Flagship example, part 3: build a real Skill using the guided "Create with Claude" path — the simplest way to build one, no file-writing required.
steps: First, confirm the prerequisite: Settings → Capabilities → check that "Code execution and file creation" is toggled on. Skills need this to work.
Go to Customize → Skills in the left sidebar (or click the "+" button and choose "Create skill").

You'll see a few creation options — choose "Create with Claude." This is a short, guided conversation where Claude interviews you about the task to build the skill for you, rather than you writing instructions from scratch.
Describe the repeatable task clearly — for example, "I write a weekly client status update, always in the same format." Answer Claude's follow-up questions about your exact format and preferences.
Once complete, save the skill. It now appears in your Skills list, ready to be used whenever a matching task comes up in future chats.

screens.promptLabel: Karan builds a real Skill for weekly client updates
screens.prompt: [Inside Create with Claude] I write a weekly client status update. It's always the same format: a one-line headline, three bullet points under 'This week,' and one line under 'Next week.' Keep it under 150 words total, no filler phrases.
screens.examplePrompt: [Inside Create with Claude] I write a weekly client status update. It's always the same format: a one-line headline, three bullet points under 'This week,' and one line under 'Next week.' Keep it under 150 words total, no filler phrases.
screens.output: The Skill is saved as "Weekly Client Update." Now, in any future conversation — inside the Client Onboarding Project or anywhere else — asking Claude to "write this week's client update: [real details]" automatically applies this exact format, without Karan re-describing the structure every single week.
screens.explanation: Notice the difference from the Project: this Skill works everywhere, for any client, not just inside one Project — because it's a reusable process, not context tied to one piece of ongoing work.

screens.instruction: Match the scope, broadest to narrowest: which layer applies to the most conversations, down to the fewest?

items.text: Memory — applies in every conversation, any topic
Skill — applies whenever this specific task comes up, across projects
Project — applies only inside this one specific piece of work

screens.explanation: Memory is the broadest — it's about you, always active. A Skill is narrower — only relevant when that specific kind of task comes up, but not tied to any one project. A Project is the narrowest — deliberately scoped to just that one piece of ongoing work.

screens.heading: Real breadth: who personalizes Claude, and how

list.label: A student
list.text: uses a Project per course to keep syllabus and notes separate; uses Memory for "I'm a visual learner, use diagrams where possible"; builds a Skill for "summarize any reading into a one-page study sheet."

list.label: A small business owner
list.text: uses a Project per major client; uses Memory for their brand's tone; builds a Skill for a recurring weekly report format.

list.label: An IT professional
list.text: uses a Project per system or codebase; uses Memory for their preferred code style and terminology; builds a Skill for writing consistent incident postmortems.

list.label: A freelancer
list.text: uses a Project per client engagement; uses Memory for their standard rate and availability info; builds a Skill for turning a call transcript into a proposal.

screens.question: You want Claude to always use bullet points and never write in first person, no matter what you're chatting about. Which layer fits best?

options.text: A new Project for every single chat
Memory — this is a standing preference about you, true across all conversations
A Skill you have to manually invoke every time
This isn't possible in Claude

screens.explanation: A universal formatting preference that should apply regardless of topic is exactly what Memory is for — set once, active everywhere, no manual invocation or project-switching needed.

screens.heading: From a document to something you can actually click
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **Artifacts** — real, interactive tools you build inside a conversation, not just documents or code snippets.

Module 4 gave you files. This module gives you something genuinely different: a working mini-application — something a user types into, clicks, and gets a live result from, rendered right in a side panel next to your chat.

You're going to build one real, working tool from scratch in this module: a bill-splitting calculator, spec'd, built, tested, and improved — the exact same process you'd use for anything else you'd want to build.

screens.heading: The Build Loop
body: Five stages, and you'll walk through every one of them this module:

list.label: Spec
list.text: describe exactly what the user does, not just what the tool contains — "the user types a number and clicks Calculate" beats "a calculator."

list.label: Build
list.text: Claude generates the working tool, live, in a side panel.

list.label: Test
list.text: actually use it — click the buttons, type real values, see if it behaves correctly.

list.label: Iterate
list.text: ask for specific changes in the same conversation — Claude updates the existing tool, it doesn't start over.

list.label: Publish
list.text: generate a shareable link, if you want others to actually use it.

screens.description: First, enable Artifacts if it isn't already on — verified against Claude's current Help Center.
steps: Click your profile icon (bottom-left corner) → Settings.
Go to the Capabilities section.
Confirm both "Artifacts" and "Code execution and file creation" are toggled on — Artifacts currently requires both to work.

This is available on Free, Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans — no separate purchase needed. One note: the dedicated Artifacts tab currently doesn't appear on mobile, so use desktop or web for this module.

screens.heading: Prompt Lab: Writing a real Spec
body: The single biggest quality difference in Artifacts comes from describing the *interaction*, not just the output. "The user types a bill amount and number of people, clicks Calculate, and sees the per-person total including tip" gives Claude something concrete to build. "A bill splitter" doesn't.

body.prompt: Build me an interactive tool: [what it does]. The user [describes the exact interaction — what they type/click, in what order, and what they see]. Include [any specific calculation, validation, or styling requirement].

screens.promptLabel: Karan builds a real bill-splitting calculator
screens.prompt: Build me an interactive tool: [what it does]. The user [interaction]. Include [requirements].
screens.examplePrompt: Build me an interactive tool: a bill-splitting calculator. The user types a total bill amount, types the number of people splitting it, selects a tip percentage from 10 to 25 percent, and clicks Calculate. The tool then shows the tip amount, the total with tip, and the exact amount each person owes. Include input validation so it doesn't break if someone enters 0 people, and make it look clean and simple, not cluttered.
screens.output: A real, working interactive tool opens in the side panel: input fields for bill amount and number of people, a tip percentage selector, and a Calculate button. Clicking it instantly displays the tip amount, the grand total, and each person's exact share. Typing 0 for the number of people shows a clear validation message instead of crashing or showing a broken calculation.
screens.explanation: This is a genuinely working tool, not a mockup — because the prompt described the exact interaction and even specified the edge case (0 people) up front, rather than leaving Claude to guess what "clean" or "working correctly" meant.

screens.question: True or False: Claude only creates something as an artifact if you explicitly ask for one — describing what you want normally in chat will never trigger it automatically.

options.text: True
False

screens.explanation: False — Claude automatically creates an artifact when content meets certain criteria: it's significant and self-contained (typically over 15 lines), and something you'd likely want to edit, iterate on, or reuse outside the conversation. You don't have to explicitly ask, though being explicit and using the Artifacts tab gives you more direct control.

screens.description: Now actually test what you built.
steps: In the artifact panel, look for two icons in the top-left: an eye icon (Preview) and a code-bracket icon (Code). Preview shows the live, working tool; Code shows the underlying source.
Stay in Preview mode and actually use the tool — type a real bill amount, pick a tip percentage, click Calculate. Confirm the math is actually correct by checking it yourself.
Try the edge case you specified — enter 0 people, or an unusually large number — and confirm the validation message shows up instead of a broken result.

If something errors out, look for a "Try fixing with Claude" button near the error — click it to automatically send the error details back to Claude for a fix. This doesn't guarantee a fix on the first try, but it's the fastest way to start.

screens.heading: Iterate — without starting over
body: Once something's working, don't start a new chat to change it — Claude keeps the same artifact updated as you reply in the same conversation.

body.prompt: [In the same conversation] Update the tool: [one specific, concrete change].

screens.promptLabel: Karan improves the calculator without rebuilding it
screens.prompt: [In the same conversation] Update the tool: [specific change].
screens.examplePrompt: [In the same conversation] Update the tool: add a currency symbol dropdown (₹, $, €) that updates all the displayed amounts, and make the Calculate button disabled until both fields have a value.
screens.output: The exact same artifact updates in place — same tool, same panel, now with a currency dropdown that changes the ₹/$/€ symbol across every displayed number, and the Calculate button greyed out until both required fields are filled in. No new artifact was created; this is a genuine update to what was already there.
screens.explanation: This matters because iterating in place preserves everything that already worked — Karan didn't have to re-describe the tip logic or the validation rule, just the one new thing he wanted changed.

screens.question: Which of these are good iteration requests? Select all that apply.

options.text: "Make the header sticky and add a loading spinner when data fetches"
"Change the tip percentage options to 15, 18, and 20 percent only"
"Make it better"
"Fix it"

screens.explanation: A and B are specific, concrete changes — exactly what makes an iteration request effective. C and D give Claude nothing to act on precisely, the same way a vague initial Spec produces a vague first build.

screens.description: Once you're happy with it, publish it so others can actually use it.
steps: In the artifact panel, look for the "Publish" button.
Click it to generate a public link.
Anyone with that link can open and use your tool — they don't need a Claude account to use a published artifact.
You can un-publish at any time from the same panel, which disables the link immediately.

screens.question: Your published expense splitter throws an error when a user types letters instead of numbers into the bill amount field. What's the fastest first move?

options.text: Delete the artifact and start over from scratch
Look for a "Try fixing with Claude" button near the error, and click it
Un-publish it permanently and never use Artifacts again
Ignore it, since errors can't be fixed

screens.explanation: This is exactly what that button exists for — it automatically sends the error details to Claude to diagnose and attempt a fix, without you needing to manually describe what went wrong. It's not guaranteed to succeed on the first try, but it's always the fastest starting point.

list.label: A student
list.text: builds a study timer with customizable work/break intervals; builds a flashcard quiz tool from their own notes.

list.label: A small business owner
list.text: builds a simple quote calculator for customers; builds an inventory reorder-point tracker.

list.label: An IT professional

list.label: A freelancer
