screens.instruction: Put the Build Loop stages in the correct order.

items.text: Spec — describe the exact user interaction
Build — Claude generates the working tool
Test — actually use it, check edge cases
Iterate — request specific changes in the same chat
Publish — generate a shareable link

screens.explanation: Skipping straight from Build to Publish without genuinely Testing is the most common mistake — an untested tool that looks fine in a glance can still break on a real user's first unexpected input, exactly like the letters-in-a-number-field example.

screens.heading: Build your own Artifact Spec
screens.template: Build me an interactive tool: [[1]]. The user [[2]], and sees [[3]] as a result.

options: types/clicks in a specific described order
blanks.correct: types/clicks in a specific described order

screens.explanation: This is the Spec stage of the Build Loop turned into a fill-in template — describing the exact interaction, step by step, is what separates a working first draft from a vague starting point that needs several rounds of guessing.

screens.heading: Your turn — build your own interactive tool
screens.prompt: Build me an interactive tool: [what it does]. The user [exact interaction — what they type/click, in order]. Include [any specific requirement or edge case].
screens.examplePrompt: Build me an interactive tool: a simple study timer. The user sets a work duration and a break duration in minutes, clicks Start, and sees a countdown that switches automatically between work and break periods with a sound or visual alert. Include a Pause and Reset button.
screens.note: Run through the whole Build Loop yourself — Spec it, Build it, actually Test it with real input, and ask for at least one real Iteration before you're done.

items: **The Build Loop** — Spec, Build, Test, Iterate, Publish — is the whole process, and skipping Test is the most common real mistake.
A good Spec describes the **exact user interaction**, not just what the tool contains — that's the biggest quality lever you have.
**Iterate in the same conversation** — Claude updates the existing artifact, it doesn't need to start over.
The **"Try fixing with Claude"** button is your fastest first move on any artifact error.

screens.heading: What you built, and what's next
body: You now have a real, working, tested, iterated, and publishable interactive tool — built from a single well-specified prompt, not a template.
**Module 7** goes one level deeper: Claude Code — building real, local, production-grade tools and scripts, not just in-browser artifacts.

modules.title: Claude as a Coding Partner
outcomes: Install and start Claude Code, and understand how it genuinely differs from everything else in this course
Build a real, working script on your own computer — spec'd, built, tested, documented, and handed off
Understand how Claude Code's approval system keeps you in control of real changes to real files
See real breadth of use across students, business owners, IT professionals, and freelancers

screens.heading: A genuinely different kind of tool
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **Claude Code**.

Everything so far in this course has run inside your browser at claude.ai. Claude Code is different — it's a separate command-line tool that runs on your own computer, works with real local files, and can actually create, edit, and run code directly on your machine.

Being honest about the bar here: this module needs a bit more technical setup than anything before it — installing Node.js and using a terminal. If you've never used a terminal before, go slowly through the install steps and don't skip the verification checks. Once it's running, the actual working part is genuinely approachable, even if you've never coded.

screens.heading: Spec, Build, Test, Document, Handoff
body: The Build Loop from Module 6 gets one real addition here — because Claude Code touches real files on your real computer, not a sandboxed browser panel:

list.label: Spec
list.text: describe exactly what the script should do, with real inputs and outputs.

list.label: Build
list.text: Claude Code writes the actual files, asking your approval before each real change.

list.label: Test
list.text: run it yourself, with real data, and check the actual result.

list.label: Document
list.text: ask Claude to write a plain README explaining what it does and how to run it — this matters far more here than in a browser artifact, since a script with no explanation is unusable to anyone but you a month from now.

list.label: Handoff
list.text: the script and its documentation are now something you (or someone else) can actually run again, independently.

screens.description: Step 1: install Claude Code. Verified against Anthropic's current official documentation.
steps: Confirm you have Node.js version 18 or higher — open a terminal (Command Prompt or PowerShell on Windows, Terminal on Mac) and type: node --version. If you don't have Node.js at all, install it from nodejs.org first (the LTS version).
In your terminal, run: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code
Windows users may also need Git installed separately — if the install step errors out, install Git for Windows from git-scm.com and try again.
Once installed, run: claude — this starts a login flow. Choose to log in with your Claude account (a one-time authentication step).
If anything goes wrong at any point, run: claude doctor — this runs a full setup checkup and can automatically fix many common issues.

screens.description: Step 2: start your first real session, in a real folder.
steps: Create a new, empty folder on your computer for this exercise — e.g. "expense-tool" — and navigate into it in your terminal (cd expense-tool).
Run: claude — this starts an interactive session, right there in that folder.
Ask a simple first question to confirm it's working — e.g. "what files are in this folder?" — Claude Code can read your current folder's contents directly.
You're now ready to give it a real task.

screens.heading: Prompt Lab: Your flagship Spec
body: Same principle as Module 6's Artifacts — describe the real inputs, the real logic, and the real output, not just the topic.

body.prompt: Write a script that [does what, with what real input] and [produces what real output]. Use [language, if you have a preference — otherwise let Claude choose]. Include basic error handling for [a realistic bad input].

screens.promptLabel: Karan builds a real expense-summary script
screens.prompt: Write a script that [reads/processes what] and [produces what output]. Include error handling for [realistic bad input].
screens.examplePrompt: Write a script that reads a CSV file of expenses (columns: Date, Category, Amount) and produces a summary showing the total spent per category, plus the overall total. Use Python. Include basic error handling for a missing or malformed Amount value — skip that row and note it, don't crash.
screens.output: Claude Code proposes creating a new file, expense_summary.py, and shows you exactly what it plans to write before doing it — asking for your approval first. Once approved, it creates the file with a working script: reads the CSV, sums amounts by category, prints a clean summary, and explicitly skips and reports any row with a bad Amount value instead of crashing.
screens.explanation: Notice the approval step before the file was actually created — this is Claude Code's default behavior, and it's the single most important safety habit in this whole module.

screens.heading: How the approval system actually works
body: By default, Claude Code asks before taking real actions — creating a file, editing one, or running a command. You'll see exactly what it's about to do, and you approve or decline each one.

list.label: Approve
list.text: the action happens exactly as shown.

list.label: Decline or ask for a change
list.text: nothing happens to your real files until you say yes.

body: ==This is the same human-in-the-loop principle from earlier modules, now applied to something with real consequences — actual files on your actual computer.==

screens.question: True or False: Claude Code silently creates, edits, and runs files without ever asking you first.

options.text: True
False

screens.explanation: False — by default, Claude Code shows you exactly what it's about to do (create a file, edit one, run a command) and asks for your approval before it happens. This default can be configured differently for advanced workflows, but the default is always review-first.

screens.description: Step 3: actually test it, with real data.
steps: Create a small, real CSV file in the same folder — a few rows of realistic expense data, including one row with a deliberately bad or missing Amount value, to test the error handling.
Ask Claude Code to run the script against your real file, or run it yourself directly in the terminal.
Check the output for real: do the category totals actually add up correctly? Did the bad row get skipped and flagged, not silently ignored or crashed on?

screens.promptLabel: Testing against real data, including a deliberate bad row
screens.prompt: Run the script against [test file], and confirm the output is correct.
screens.examplePrompt: Run the script against expenses_test.csv, which has 6 rows including one with a blank Amount. Confirm the totals are correct and the bad row is flagged, not crashed on.
screens.output: Output shows category totals correctly calculated across the 5 valid rows, an overall total, and a clear printed note: "Skipped row 4: missing Amount value." The script didn't crash and didn't silently drop the problem — it surfaced it.
screens.explanation: This is exactly what a good Spec, tested properly, gets you — a script that fails safely and tells you why, instead of either crashing entirely or quietly producing a wrong total.

screens.heading: Document — the step people skip, and shouldn't

body.prompt: Write a short README for this script: what it does, how to run it, what input format it expects, and what to do if it errors out.

screens.promptLabel: Getting a real README, not just a working script
screens.prompt: Write a short README for this script: what it does, how to run it, expected input format, and what to do if it errors out.
screens.examplePrompt: Write a short README for this script: what it does, how to run it, expected input format, and what to do if it errors out.
screens.output: A README.md file explaining in plain language: what the script does, the exact command to run it, the expected CSV column names and format, and what the "skipped row" message means if it appears.
screens.explanation: A script with no documentation is only usable by the person who just built it, and only while they still remember exactly how it works. This one file is the difference between a tool Karan can hand to a colleague and one only he can ever use.

screens.question: Karan wants to hand this script to a colleague who's never used it. What's the most important thing to check before he does?

options.text: Nothing — the script working on his own machine is enough
That the README clearly explains how to run it and what input format it expects, so the colleague doesn't need Karan to explain it in person
That the code is written in the most advanced style possible
That the script never asks for approval on anything

screens.explanation: This is the entire point of the Document and Handoff stages — a working script that only makes sense to the person who built it isn't actually reusable. Clear documentation is what makes it genuinely handoff-ready.

screens.heading: Real breadth: who uses Claude Code, and for what

list.label: A student
list.text: builds a small script to rename and organize downloaded research PDFs consistently; automates reformatting citation lists.

list.label: A small business owner
list.text: builds a script like Karan's expense summarizer; automates converting between two file formats their tools don't handle natively.

list.label: An IT professional
list.text: builds and maintains real internal tools and automation scripts, with Claude Code handling routine refactoring and bug fixes under review.

list.label: A freelancer
list.text: builds a script to batch-rename and organize client deliverable files consistently before delivery.

screens.instruction: Put the stages in the correct order.

items.text: Spec — describe the real inputs, logic, and output
Build — Claude Code writes the files, with your approval
Test — run it against real data, including bad input
Document — write a README explaining it
Handoff — someone else can now use it independently

screens.explanation: Documentation has to come after real testing, not before — you can't accurately document behavior you haven't actually verified yet, especially the error-handling behavior.

screens.heading: Build your own Claude Code spec
screens.template: Write a script that [[1]] and [[2]]. Include error handling for [[3]].

options: a realistic bad input you can actually test
every possible error in the universe
blanks.correct: a realistic bad input you can actually test

screens.explanation: This is the Spec stage turned into a fill-in template — specific real input, specific real output, and one realistic failure case you can actually test, not an impossibly broad request to handle every conceivable error.

screens.heading: Your turn — build, test, and document your own script
screens.prompt: Write a script that [your real repetitive task] and [real output]. Include error handling for [a realistic bad input]. Then test it against real data, and ask for a README.
screens.examplePrompt: Write a script that renames all image files in a folder to a consistent format (e.g. photo-001.jpg, photo-002.jpg) based on their current date, keeping the original file extension. Include error handling for files with no readable date. Then test it on a real test folder, and ask for a README.
screens.note: Run through all five stages for real — Spec, Build (approving each real action), Test with real data including one deliberately bad case, and Document. Don't skip Document, even though it's tempting once the script works.

items: Claude Code works with **real local files on your real computer** — genuinely different from the sandboxed browser artifacts in Module 6.
**Spec, Build, Test, Document, Handoff** — Document is the stage people skip, and it's what makes a script reusable by anyone other than the person who built it.
**Claude Code asks for approval before real actions** by default — the same human-in-the-loop principle from earlier modules, now with real consequences.
Test with **realistic bad input on purpose** — a script that fails safely and tells you why is far more trustworthy than one that's only ever seen perfect data.

screens.heading: What you built, and what's next
body: You now have a real, tested, documented script running on your own computer — built through an approval process you controlled at every step.
**Module 8** shifts from you approving each step to something more autonomous: Cowork, and the tiers of delegation that decide how much Claude can do on its own.

modules.title: Delegating Work
outcomes: Understand Cowork's three permission modes and why Manual is always the right starting point
Delegate a real, multi-step task and watch Claude work through it, approving actions along the way
Set up Global Instructions so you stop repeating the same context every session
See real breadth of use across students, business owners, IT professionals, and freelancers

screens.heading: From approving each step to describing the outcome
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **Cowork**.

In Module 7, you approved every single file change one at a time. Cowork is built for a different kind of task: you describe the finished outcome, step away, and come back to real work done — across multiple steps, multiple tools, and potentially several minutes or longer.
One thing worth knowing upfront: **Cowork requires a paid plan** (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise) — it isn't available on the free tier, unlike most of what this course has covered so far.

screens.heading: The Trust Ladder
body: Cowork has three permission modes, and picking the right one is the single most important safety decision you'll make in this module:

list.label: Manual
list.text: Claude pauses and asks before each real action. Start here, always — especially the first time you run any new task.

list.label: Auto
list.text: Claude self-reviews each step and blocks anything it judges unsafe, without pausing for your approval on routine steps. Uses more of your usage allocation, since it's doing extra safety-checking itself.

list.label: Skip
list.text: no pauses, no automatic safety checks. Reserved for low-risk, well-understood, already-tested tasks only.

body: ==Never schedule or run in Skip mode a task you haven't already tested carefully in Manual first.==
One protection applies no matter which mode you're in: Claude always requires your explicit permission before permanently deleting any files.

screens.description: Step 1: set up Global Instructions, so you stop repeating context every session — Cowork doesn't carry regular chat memory between sessions by default.
steps: Go to Settings → Cowork → Edit Global Instructions.

Write your standing context here: your general tone/style preferences, any file-naming conventions you use, and anything that should always be off-limits (e.g. "never touch anything in the Archive folder").
Save. Every future Cowork session will now start with this context already applied, without you retyping it.

screens.description: Step 2: start your flagship task, in Manual mode.
steps: In the message box, select "Cowork" (Cowork and regular chat now share the same message box).
Confirm the mode selector shows "Manual" — this is the default and the correct starting choice.
Describe the outcome you want, not just a single instruction — Cowork works best with a real, describable finished result in mind.
Send it, and watch — Cowork will show its reasoning and plan as it goes, pausing to ask permission before each real action.

screens.promptLabel: Takshika delegates a real file-organization task
screens.prompt: [Cowork, Manual mode] Organize my [folder]: [describe the desired end state clearly].
screens.examplePrompt: [Cowork, Manual mode] Organize my Training Materials folder: group files by topic into subfolders, rename anything with unclear names to something descriptive based on its content, and flag (don't delete) anything that looks like a duplicate.
screens.output: Cowork works through the folder, pausing to show its plan and ask permission before creating new subfolders and before renaming each batch of files. When it identifies two files that look like duplicates, it flags them clearly in a summary rather than deleting either one — exactly matching the built-in deletion protection. When finished, it presents a summary of every change made.
screens.explanation: Notice what happened with the possible duplicates — Cowork didn't just quietly remove one. Deletion always requires explicit permission, regardless of mode, which is exactly the kind of guardrail worth understanding before you delegate anything real.

screens.question: True or False: even in Skip mode, Cowork will still ask your explicit permission before permanently deleting a file.

options.text: True
False

screens.explanation: True — deletion protection applies regardless of which permission mode you're in. You'll always see a permission prompt and need to select "Allow" before Cowork performs any permanent deletion.

screens.heading: Connectors inside Cowork
body: Cowork can use the same Connectors from Module 2 — controlled via the "+" menu in the chat box, or Customize → Connectors, exactly like before. This is where Cowork's real power shows up: a task that reads your calendar, cross-references a project tracker, and drafts a summary — all in one delegated run, instead of three separate manual conversations.
In Manual mode, Cowork will pause and ask permission the first time it uses each connector in a session — approve it the same way you'd approve a file action.

screens.question: Which of these are genuine Cowork safety mechanics? Select all that apply.

options.text: Manual mode pauses before every real action
Deletion always requires explicit permission, in every mode
Auto mode has Claude self-review steps and block unsafe actions
Cowork automatically remembers everything from your last regular chat conversation

screens.explanation: A, B, and C are all real, verified mechanics. D is false — Cowork does not carry regular chat memory into sessions by default, which is exactly why Global Instructions exist as the way to set standing context.

screens.heading: Scheduling — but only after real testing
body: Once a task genuinely works in Manual mode, you can schedule it to run automatically — on Anthropic's servers, so your computer doesn't need to stay on.

body.prompt: /schedule [describe the task and how often it should run]

screens.description: How to actually schedule a task, once tested:
steps: Click "Scheduled" in the left sidebar.
Click "New task" in the upper right, then choose "Create with Claude" — this starts a guided conversation where Claude asks what you want and how often.
Claude will confirm the task name, the schedule, and exactly what it does before creating it — click "Schedule" to confirm.
Always click "Run now" first to test a newly scheduled task manually, rather than waiting for its first automatic run — this is the same test-before-trust principle from every module before this one.

screens.question: You just built a Cowork task in Manual mode and it worked perfectly. What's the recommended next step before scheduling it to run weekly?

options.text: Schedule it immediately in Skip mode for maximum speed
Nothing more is needed — one successful Manual run means it's ready for anything
Consider testing it a few more times, and only move to a less-supervised mode once you genuinely trust its behavior across different real situations
Delete it and start over

screens.explanation: One successful run is a good sign, not a guarantee — real-world tasks encounter different data and edge cases over time. Building genuine trust before loosening supervision is the same principle covered across every module in this course.

screens.heading: Real breadth: who delegates to Cowork, and for what

list.label: A student
list.text: delegates organizing a semester's worth of downloaded readings into topic folders; schedules a weekly summary of upcoming deadlines from a connected calendar.

list.label: A small business owner
list.text: delegates weekly cross-referencing of orders against inventory; schedules a Monday competitor-news briefing.

list.label: An IT professional
list.text: delegates routine log-file organization and flagging of anomalies; schedules a recurring system status summary for stakeholders.

list.label: A freelancer
list.text: delegates organizing client deliverables before a handoff; schedules a weekly check of upcoming project deadlines across multiple connected tools.

screens.instruction: Put these in the correct order, from most supervised to least.

items.text: Manual — Claude pauses before every action
Auto — Claude self-reviews, blocks unsafe actions

screens.heading: You've learned eight surfaces. Now combine them.
body: Claude functionality covered in this module: **Workflow Design** — no single new feature this time. Instead, you're combining Connectors, Research, File Creation, and Skills — everything from Modules 2 through 5 — into one real, repeatable system.

Every module so far taught one capability in isolation. Real work rarely stays inside one box. This module builds the actual habit of asking: which surface handles each step, and where might the handoffs between them break?

list.label: Design

screens.heading: Clarify: Karan's real goal
body: Karan doesn't actually want "a report." He wants to walk into his Monday team meeting already knowing what's overdue, whether a competitor changed anything worth reacting to, and having something to hand his manager without spending an hour writing it himself.
That's the real goal underneath the request — and it's what should drive which surfaces get used, not the other way around.

screens.heading: Design: mapping the steps to surfaces

list.label: Step 1 — pull real current data
list.text: his connected project tracker (Module 2: Connectors) — what's overdue, right now.

list.label: Step 2 — check something external
list.text: a quick competitor check (Module 3: Research) — has anything changed worth reacting to.

list.label: Step 3 — produce something he can actually hand over
list.text: a real Word document (Module 4: File Creation) — combining both into one clean report.

body: Three different surfaces, three different jobs, one real outcome — this is the entire point of Workflow Design.

screens.promptLabel: Step 1: pull real current data via Connector
screens.prompt: Using [connected project tracker], find all tasks overdue as of today. For each, note the task, owner, and how overdue it is.
screens.examplePrompt: Using my connected project tracker, find all tasks overdue as of today. For each, note the task, owner, and how overdue it is.
screens.output: A list of 4 currently overdue tasks, each with owner and days overdue — the exact same Connector pattern from Module 2, now feeding into something bigger instead of standing alone.
screens.explanation: Nothing new here technically — this is Module 2's skill, reused as step 1 of a longer chain rather than the whole task.

screens.promptLabel: Step 2: check something external via Research
screens.prompt: Research: has [competitor/topic] announced or changed anything in the last 7 days that I should know about? Keep it brief — 2-3 sentences.
screens.examplePrompt: Research: has my main competitor in operations consulting announced or changed anything in the last 7 days that I should know about? Keep it brief — 2-3 sentences.
screens.output: A short, cited summary: no major changes found this week, with a note on the last real update from two weeks prior, so Karan knows the space is quiet rather than wondering if the check simply failed to find anything.
screens.explanation: Notice this uses Module 3's Research skill, deliberately scoped small (2-3 sentences, not a full report) — because inside a bigger workflow, this step's job is a quick check, not a deep investigation.

screens.promptLabel: Step 3: combine both into a real Word report
screens.prompt: Create a Word document: a Monday status brief. Shape: overdue tasks section, competitor check section, one-line summary at the top. Fill: [paste both outputs from steps 1 and 2]. Finish: clean, scannable, no fluff.
screens.examplePrompt: Create a Word document: a Monday status brief. Shape: overdue tasks section, competitor check section, one-line summary at the top. Fill: [pasted the overdue task list and the competitor check]. Finish: clean, scannable, no fluff.
screens.output: A downloadable Word document opening with a one-line summary ("4 tasks overdue, no competitor changes this week"), followed by a clearly formatted overdue-tasks section and a short competitor-check section — Module 4's Shape, Fill, Finish structure, now assembling two other surfaces' outputs into one document.
screens.explanation: This is the actual payoff of Workflow Design: three separate capabilities, each doing what it's genuinely best at, combining into one deliverable Karan can hand to his manager without writing a word of it himself.

screens.question: Why does this workflow use Research for the competitor check specifically, instead of just asking Claude directly in the Word-creation prompt?

options.text: It doesn't matter — either approach works identically
Research is what actually checks live, current, external information — the File Creation step is just for formatting, not for looking anything up
Word documents can't contain researched information
This is unnecessarily complicated for no reason

screens.explanation: This is the core skill of Workflow Design — matching each step to the surface actually built for that job. Asking a file-creation prompt to also research live external information would either fail or produce an unverified guess; Research exists specifically for that step.

screens.heading: Stress-Test: where this could actually break
body: Before trusting any multi-step workflow, ask where a handoff between steps could fail — this reuses the failure-mode thinking from every earlier module, now applied across the whole chain:

list.label: Step 1 → Step 2 handoff
list.text: if the Connector pull is stale (Module 2's Staleness check), the whole report opens with wrong information, and nothing downstream would catch it.

list.label: Step 2 alone
list.text: if the Research step finds nothing, is that because nothing happened, or because the search itself failed quietly? Worth explicitly asking for a "nothing found" statement rather than silence.

list.label: Step 3
list.text: if Karan pastes the outputs in the wrong order or misses one, the Word document would look complete while actually being wrong.

screens.question: Which of these are genuine stress-test questions worth asking about a multi-step workflow like this one? Select all that apply.

options.text: Could the data feeding step 1 be stale by the time step 3 uses it?
Would I actually notice if step 2 silently failed to find anything, versus genuinely finding nothing?
Does the final document clearly distinguish what's confirmed versus what's uncertain?
None of this matters once a workflow works once

screens.explanation: A, B, and C are all real stress-test questions worth running on any multi-step chain. D is exactly the mistake this stage exists to prevent — a workflow that worked once hasn't been proven reliable across the different real situations it'll actually encounter.

screens.heading: Document: turning this into a Skill
body: Once a workflow is genuinely tested, don't rebuild the three-step chain from scratch every Monday — this is exactly what a Skill (Module 5) is for.

body.prompt: [Inside Create with Claude, building a Skill] Every Monday, I run a 3-step workflow: pull overdue tasks from my connected project tracker, do a brief 7-day competitor check, and combine both into a Word status brief with a one-line summary at the top. Turn this into a repeatable Skill.

screens.promptLabel: Building the Skill from the tested workflow
screens.prompt: [Inside Create with Claude] Every [frequency], I run this workflow: [step 1], [step 2], [step 3]. Turn this into a repeatable Skill.
screens.examplePrompt: Every Monday, I run a 3-step workflow: pull overdue tasks from my connected project tracker, do a brief 7-day competitor check, and combine both into a Word status brief with a one-line summary at the top. Turn this into a repeatable Skill.
screens.output: A new Skill, "Monday Status Brief," is saved. Future Mondays, Karan can invoke it directly instead of running three separate prompts — the Skill carries the whole sequence, including the specific Shape/Fill/Finish instructions for the final document.
screens.explanation: This is the loop closing completely: a tested, stress-tested, three-surface workflow becomes one reusable asset, exactly the way Module 5 described Skills working — now demonstrated on something genuinely useful, not a toy example.

screens.question: Why turn a working multi-step workflow into a Skill, rather than just keeping the three prompts saved somewhere to copy-paste each week?

options.text: There's no real difference between the two approaches
A Skill can be invoked directly and reliably applies the whole sequence, rather than relying on Karan remembering to run all three steps in the right order every time
Copy-pasting prompts is always faster than using a Skill
Skills can only be used once

screens.explanation: A Skill encodes the whole tested sequence as one reusable unit — removing the risk of Karan forgetting a step, running them out of order, or losing the saved prompts entirely somewhere in his notes.
